newsitem.title: UK: Stg setback temporary, bull trend intact-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Stg setback temporary, bull trend intact-analysts.

text.p: Sterling climbed back against major currencies on Friday after falling on weak U.K. asset markets the day before, and analysts said its strength was still intact despite Thursday's sudden drop.
Recent economic data showing healthiness in Britain"s economy, allied with expectations of a rise in key interest rates soon are still supporting sterling after its temporary weakness, they said.
"All the evidence points one way today, which is for a stronger sterling," said UBS senior currency economist Peter von Maydell.
"People were getting nervous over equities and trying to sell it off. They've seen sterling sold off in the past in equity market corrections," Maydell said.
U.K. stock and government bond markets suffered substantial losses on Thursday afternoon, led by their U.S. counterparts which fell on the back of strong NAPM data.
This weakness triggered selling of sterling across the board, with the pound falling to $1.6885/95 and 2.6067 marks by late European trade from the day's highs of $1.7130 and 2.6415 marks.

But analysts and traders did not think this meant sterling"s rally had ground to a halt, saying very thin volume -- many participants were still away for New Year holidays -- and the pound's volatility contributed to Thursday's big drop.
"That is always the danger with sterling, you take your eyes off it for five minutes and it's come down two or three big figures," one trader said.
By the European afternoon on Friday, the pound had recovered to $1.6950/60 and 2.6310/20 marks.
Long-held expectations of a rise in British interest rates, perhaps as early as January 15, should continue to be the major driving force for sterling's bullish trend, analysts said.
Chancellor Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George hold their next monthly monetary meeting on January 15.
Some, however, warned that such interest rate speculation may be overdone.

"The market's getting ahead of itself in terms of rates," said HSBC James Capel's U.K. economist David Bloom. "The market's expecting maybe two interest rate hikes before the (May) elections. It might be disappointed."
